My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.51 remains $0.04 (7.3%) below the consensus of $0.55, reflecting a more realistic assessment of tax rate normalization and equipment revenue seasonality that I believe Wall Street is underweighting. The core issue is Q4 2025's anomalously low 2.6% effective tax rate ($109M on $4.26B pretax income) was driven by discrete tax benefits that will not recur in Q1. Normalizing to AT&T's guided 21% effective tax rate creates approximately $780M of incremental tax expense versus Q4, which alone accounts for the majority of my below-consensus view. Additionally, equipment revenue typically declines 15-20% sequentially from Q4's holiday peak, which I'm modeling as a $4.2B contribution versus Q4's implied $5.0B+.

The Street appears to be extrapolating from Q4's 10.6% beat without adequately discounting the unsustainable nature of that outperformance. AT&T's operational momentum remains solid - fiber net adds should continue at ~250K pace, postpaid phone churn remains industry-leading, and business connectivity is stabilizing. However, these positive trends are already priced into consensus and don't offset the mechanical compression from tax normalization. Management's conservative guidance history (average 8%+ beat over last 5 quarters) suggests some sandbagging, but the Q1 tax headwind is too substantial to fully overcome.

I would revise my estimate higher if: (1) management signals at the Barclays conference that Q1 tax rate will remain depressed below 21%, (2) equipment revenue shows unusual strength in January-February, or (3) there's evidence of significant one-time gains offsetting the tax headwind. Conversely, I would lower estimates if competitive intensity manifests in ARPU compression or if working capital dynamics prove worse than modeled.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 FY2026 forecast of -$0.05 EPS on $295M revenue reflects a significant divergence from the apparent Wall Street consensus of -$0.22 EPS. The key differentiation lies in my expectation that Tilray will NOT record another major non-cash impairment charge this quarter. The company took massive goodwill impairments in Q4 2025 ($1.75B) and Q3 2025 ($1.14B), which artificially inflated headline EPS losses to -$18 and -$13 per share respectively. With goodwill now written down to ~$1.05B and no obvious triggering events, I expect Q3 to reflect operational performance without major non-cash charges.

Operationally, Tilray has stabilized around breakeven to slightly negative EBITDA territory. Q1 FY2026 showed near-breakeven EPS (-$0.00) on $288M revenue, while Q2 showed elevated losses (-$0.57 EPS on $304M revenue) primarily due to a $14M spike in SG&A from $88M to $102M. My thesis assumes SG&A partially normalizes to ~$94M in Q3 as some of the Q2 spike was likely one-time in nature (potentially related to severance, professional fees, or integration costs). Revenue should moderate slightly to $295M as Q3 typically shows seasonal softness in beverage alcohol.

The key risks to my thesis are: (1) SG&A remains elevated at $102M+, which would push EPS toward -$0.12; (2) Another unexpected impairment charge which would dramatically worsen headline EPS; (3) Cannabis pricing deteriorates faster than expected. If any of these materialize, I would revise my estimate downward. However, the Molson Coors transcript mentioning craft beer struggles is neutral to slightly bearish for Tilray's beverage segment, but doesn't change my overall outlook materially.

Now EIGHT days have passed since the Feb 19 virtual roadshow with CEO Mullowney and CFO Leonard, yet there has been ZERO public disclosure addressing the tax situation that caused Q1's 111% effective tax rate ($7.0M tax expense on $6.3M pre-tax income). The Street's $0.02 consensus implicitly assumes a ~30-35% effective tax rate normalization - but this assumption is demonstrably unrealistic based on actual Q1 results and the structural nature of Tanzania's mining taxes (royalties, withholding taxes, and deferred tax timing).

Operationally, TRX Gold continues to execute well at Buckreef. Revenue has grown from $13M in Q2 2025 to $35M in Q1 2026 (+169% YoY), gross margins remain excellent at 56%, and the production ramp trajectory supports my $38M revenue estimate for Q2. However, the disconnect between operational excellence and bottom-line profitability is the critical variant perception the Street is missing. Roth Capital's $2.25 price target (80% upside from current levels) focuses entirely on operational thesis and long-term resource value - yet provides no analysis of the tax regime that consumed 111% of pre-tax income in Q1.

I would revise my estimate upward if: (1) Management provides specific guidance on expected effective tax rate normalization with supporting regulatory/legal evidence; (2) Q2 actual results show tax rate below 50%; or (3) Tanzania government announces mining tax relief measures. Until then, my 56% effective tax rate assumption (conservative relative to Q1's 111%) reflects structural realities that Wall Street is ignoring. The stock's 11% rally on analyst upgrades without fundamental disclosure represents momentum trading, not informed investment thesis validation.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.73 remains 4.3% above consensus of $0.70, reflecting continued conviction in UCB's NIM expansion trajectory and confidence that Q4's elevated operating expenses were largely non-recurring. The key differentiation from Street estimates centers on three factors: (1) net interest income will continue its upward trajectory to approximately $242M (+1.7% QoQ) as the loan book reprices at higher yields while deposit costs have clearly stabilized around $108M following the $12M decline from Q3 to Q4, (2) SG&A will normalize from Q4's elevated $103.5M back toward the $97-98M run-rate as one-time items (likely related to new commercial banking leadership hiring and year-end accruals) roll off, and (3) continued active capital return through the buyback program will modestly support EPS.

The Street appears anchored to Q4's slight EPS miss (-1.4% surprise at $0.70 vs $0.71 expected), but that miss was driven by operating expense timing rather than fundamental weakness. Revenue actually beat with 11% YoY growth, and credit quality metrics remained pristine per management's commentary on NPAs, past dues, and substandard loans. The appointment of Sharon Thompson as Chief Commercial Banking Officer signals management's confidence in the growth outlook, while institutional buying (Public Sector Pension Investment Board increasing stake 14.4%) provides external validation. My model shows Q1 revenue of $416M (+3.1% QoQ, +13.6% YoY) with operating income of $118M and net income of approximately $89M to the bottom line.

What would change my view: If Q1 earnings commentary reveals (1) deposit cost pressures re-emerging, (2) material deterioration in CRE credit quality requiring higher provisions, or (3) indication that elevated Q4 expenses represent a new run-rate rather than timing items. The primary swing factor is operating expense normalization - if SG&A remains above $100M, my estimate would need to come down by approximately $0.02-0.03. However, based on the pattern of historical expense levels and management's lack of guidance suggesting structural cost increases, I maintain high conviction in the expense normalization thesis.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $1.24 represents a modest 2.5% premium to Street consensus of $1.21, reflecting my view that UniFirst's stable recurring revenue model and improving operating leverage will deliver marginally above-consensus performance. The key differentiator in my model is the assumption of gross margin recovery to approximately 35.0% from Q2 2025's seasonal trough of 34.6%, driven by improved route density optimization, moderating fuel costs year-over-year, and effective contractual price escalators that have been successfully passed through to customers. This gross margin assumption is supported by Vestis's Q1 2026 results reaffirming their fiscal 2026 outlook, signaling stable industry-wide demand and pricing power.

The ongoing Cintas acquisition discussions remain the dominant variable for the stock but have limited near-term impact on operational execution. Management has historically demonstrated disciplined cost control, and while I expect M&A advisory fees to create $1-2M of incremental SG&A pressure, this is partially offset by reduced share repurchase activity preserving cash optionality. My revenue estimate of $627.5M implies 4.2% year-over-year growth, consistent with the company's historical 3-4% organic growth rate plus small tuck-in acquisition contributions. The uniform rental industry remains resilient with limited cyclicality, providing earnings visibility that supports my medium-conviction call.

What would change my view: If Q2 operating expenses come in materially higher than expected due to elevated M&A advisory costs or integration expenses from recent acquisitions, I would need to reduce my estimate. Alternatively, if the Cintas deal progresses to a definitive agreement, the forecast becomes secondary to merger arbitrage considerations. My $0.03 premium to consensus reflects confidence in operational execution rather than any heroic assumptions about acceleration.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.58 remains 15.3% above the stale Street consensus of $1.37, reflecting continued conviction that analysts are systematically underestimating Unity Bancorp's earnings power. The 7% dividend increase announced on February 26, 2026 (to $0.16/share) reinforces management's confidence in sustained profitability and capital generation. This marks another signal that the bank's fundamentals remain robust - you don't raise dividends if you see earnings pressure ahead. The four consecutive significant earnings beats (+0% Q1, +36.4% Q2, +9.3% Q3, +11.8% Q4 2025) demonstrate that Street models consistently fail to capture Unity's superior net interest margin franchise operating at 4.5% versus peer average of 3.2-3.5%.

The key differentiated insight driving my above-consensus estimate is the persistence of Unity's NIM advantage in a stabilizing rate environment. While many community banks have seen NIM compression, Unity's disciplined deposit pricing and commercial/residential loan mix have preserved spreads. The loan portfolio is growing 10-12% YoY per management commentary, driving NII higher. With Q4 2025 net interest income at $31.4M and loan growth continuing, I project Q1 2026 NII of $32.5M. Combined with stable non-interest income of ~$5.5M and controlled operating expenses (~$15.8M), this supports net income of ~$15.8M and diluted EPS of $1.58.

What would make me wrong: (1) Unexpected NIM compression from competitive deposit pricing pressures - I'm watching deposit betas closely; (2) Credit deterioration in the CRE portfolio, though Q4 2025 NPL ratios showed no stress; (3) Management sandbagging through conservative provisioning. The CEO's modest stock sale ($81,750, 0.86% of holdings) is de minimis and doesn't signal concern. I maintain high conviction that Street estimates have not caught up to Unity's demonstrated earnings trajectory.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.58 remains 3% below the Street consensus of $1.63, reflecting a continued cautious view on seasonal refining margin compression that I believe consensus is underweighting. While I've revised slightly upward from my prior $1.55 estimate based on mid-quarter crack spread data holding at $14-15/bbl (better than initial $12-14 fears) and confirmed Venezuelan crude feedstock advantages, Q1 remains historically Valero's weakest quarter. The catastrophic Q1 2025 (-$1.90 EPS loss) demonstrates the operational leverage to the downside, and while current conditions are meaningfully better, the Street appears to be extrapolating Q4's strong $3.82 EPS beat without adequately discounting the ~20% seasonal compression in crack spreads and elevated turnaround activity.

The key variant perception is that consensus is overweighting the Venezuelan crude benefit while underweighting the continued drag from renewable diesel operations. The 6.5M barrel Venezuelan crude import in March provides a $2-3/bbl feedstock advantage, but this translates to only ~$15-20M in quarterly savings - not a game-changer. Meanwhile, the renewable diesel segment continues to hemorrhage $150-180M quarterly as the SAF transition remains challenging. Management's commentary in the Q4 call about 'transition headwinds' in renewable fuels suggests no near-term relief. Additionally, the Ardmore refinery lawsuits represent a modest but real contingent liability that could eventually impact results.

I would revise my estimate upward if: (1) crack spreads strengthen to $16+/bbl through February-March, (2) turnaround activity comes in lighter than scheduled, or (3) renewable diesel shows unexpected improvement. Conversely, risks to the downside include crack spread deterioration below $13/bbl, Venezuelan sanctions risk materializing, or significant legal/regulatory costs from the Ardmore or Benicia situations. My confidence level is moderate (0.62) given the inherent volatility in refining margins and the significant swing factor that Q1 historically represents.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.15 is 5.0% below the Street consensus of $1.21, reflecting a more conservative assessment of three compounding headwinds that the market is underweighting. First, the January 2026 network outage that CEO Dan Schulman explicitly acknowledged as a 'customer service failure' on the earnings call will create measurable Q1 churn headwinds and remediation costs. Based on historical outage impacts at telecom carriers, I estimate 50-75bps incremental postpaid phone churn plus approximately $75M in customer credits and network remediation costs. The CEO's candid acknowledgment signals this was a material event. Second, while management claims the Frontier integration is 'proceeding ahead of schedule,' first-quarter integrations historically underperform due to systems complexity; I'm modeling $850M revenue contribution vs the implied $1.0B, plus front-loaded integration costs of $150-200M. Third, the €2.25B and £600M subordinated note issuances in February add approximately $80-100M to quarterly interest expense that isn't fully reflected in consensus models.

The additional CEO insider selling this week (200,000 shares at $49.61 on February 24th, reducing his direct stake by 58%) reinforces my cautious stance. While insider sales often have benign explanations, the magnitude and timing—near a 52-week high and post-outage—is notable. Combined with yesterday's 225,000 share sale, the CEO has reduced exposure by over $21M in a single week. Institutional flows are mixed (TD Asset Management reduced by 6%, Mitsubishi UFJ increased 4.6%), suggesting smart money is divided on near-term direction.

What would change my view: Evidence that churn metrics in January-February normalized quickly (management commentary on Q1 call), Frontier revenue contribution exceeding $950M with clean integration, or a clearer path to synergy realization. If Q1 shows subscriber momentum resilience despite the outage, I would revise my H2 estimates upward. The 6.5% dividend yield provides downside protection, but the $49.80 analyst target near current price suggests limited near-term upside until execution concerns are addressed.

My view would be challenged if the Q4 charge was primarily asset impairments with no cash-cost benefit, or if the debt increase signals a fundamental cash flow shortfall rather than strategic pre-funding. However, the data points to a margin-expansion story masked by headline noise.

My Q4 2025 forecast for Waldencast remains at -$0.14 EPS on $135M revenue, unchanged from my previous estimate due to the complete absence of any new information. The now 5+ week earnings delay without any company communication remains the most significant signal, strongly suggesting material issues with audit completion, potential restatement requirements, or going concern qualification discussions. While I expect the underlying business showed modest sequential improvement from Q2 2025's impairment-driven disaster - with Milk Makeup benefiting from prestige beauty resilience and holiday seasonality offsetting continued Obagi professional channel weakness - the information vacuum prevents any meaningful update to my forecast.

My differentiated view centers on the probability distribution around outcomes being highly non-normal. The consensus of -$0.12 EPS assumes relatively clean operations, but the extended reporting delay suggests we could see either: (1) material audit adjustments/restatements, (2) additional impairment charges on remaining goodwill/intangibles, (3) going concern qualification, or (4) disclosure of financing terms that significantly dilute shareholders. I'm maintaining -$0.14 EPS as my base case, slightly worse than consensus, reflecting elevated legal/audit costs and continued operational challenges, but with unusually wide confidence intervals.

The critical watch item remains the cash position. My model projects approximately $5M ending cash, which is existentially insufficient for a company with $15M+ quarterly cash burn. The financing that will be disclosed alongside Q4 results - whenever they're finally released - will likely be highly dilutive and could materially alter the per-share economics going forward. I would revise my view upward if the company reports clean results with a reasonable financing structure, or downward if we see additional impairments, going concern language, or evidence of accelerating operational deterioration.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 WFC EPS estimate of $1.58 sits modestly above the Street's $1.56 consensus (+1.3%), reflecting a balanced view that appropriately weights both the headwinds and tailwinds facing the bank. The Street is correctly cautious on NII compression (I project ~$11.45B, down 7% QoQ), but I believe analysts are slightly underweighting the wealth management fee uplift from tax season's $150B liquidity deployment and the continued benefit from aggressive share repurchases reducing diluted count to ~3.19B. The 10-K filed 2026-02-24 confirms management's commitment to capital return, validating the buyback trajectory that continues to provide meaningful EPS support.

I've reduced my estimate slightly from my prior $1.59 forecast after more carefully modeling the Q1 seasonal expense reset. Historical patterns show Q1 expenses typically rise $300-400M from Q4 due to compensation and benefits resets, and the elevated selling/administrative expenses in Q4 ($12.12B) suggest some Q1 true-up may have been pulled forward but not all. Additionally, I'm now modeling a more conservative NII trajectory at $11.45B versus my prior $11.50B assumption, given continued Fed rate cut expectations and potential deposit migration acceleration. The credit outlook remains benign based on recent 8-K filings showing no material deterioration signals.

The key swing factor is NII trajectory - if deposit repricing accelerates faster than loan yields compress, there could be $0.02-0.03 upside to my estimate. Conversely, if commercial real estate stress materializes or investment banking activity slows more than expected, there's equivalent downside risk. My revenue forecast of 148.5B JPY stands ~12% above consensus. Wall Street appears to be anchoring on general industrial weakness (China) while missing the specific, high-velocity turn in the memory/logic capex cycle. Historically, Yaskawa's Q4 benefits from budget flushes and seasonal strength, contradicting the bearish sequential decline implied by consensus. I project operating leverage to deliver EPS of 47.72 JPY, beating the street's 46.39 JPY.

Intellectual honesty requires acknowledging that if China's general automation demand deteriorated significantly in Jan/Feb, it could offset the semi-cap gains. However, the 'smoking gun' of MKS Instruments' recent guidance hike gives me high conviction that the motion control segment will outperform expectations.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view stays modestly below consensus EPS: the Street’s 46.39 implies a cleaner Robotics rebound and/or stronger operating leverage than I’m willing to underwrite without Yaskawa-specific order/backlog or margin commentary. I model Robotics as stabilizing with only a mild sequential improvement, while Motion Control provides steadier support and typical Q4 seasonality lifts revenue.

Quantitatively, I’m forecasting revenue of 140.2B and EPS of 44.7, with operating income of 14.1B and total other income/expense net of -0.22B. I would change my mind (and move closer to/above consensus) if there is credible evidence of a Robotics order/backlog acceleration or sustained margin expansion (mix/price/absorption) that supports higher operating leverage; conversely, a renewed Robotics destock or unfavorable FX/non-op would push realized EPS further below my estimate.
